sections.title: Cognition beyond the skin

source_span.end_text: Cognitive processes ain't (all) in the head!

sections.summary: Mental rotation, Tetris, writing, and other external aids motivate a parity argument: operations that would count as cognitive inside the head can also count when performed through the environment. Epistemic actions alter the world to support recognition and reasoning.

sections.title: Active coupling and objections to extended cognition

source_span.start_text: In these cases, the human organism
source_span.end_text: extended cognition is a core cognitive process, not an add-on extra.

sections.summary: Active externalism treats organism and reliably coupled resources as one cognitive system, distinguishing present causal involvement from standard externalism about meaning. Replies to consciousness and portability objections draw on reliable access, evolution, learning, and language.

sections.title: External memory as standing belief

source_span.start_text: So far we have spoken largely
source_span.end_text: and is more useful in explanation.

sections.summary: Inga’s biological memory and Otto’s notebook can play the same action-guiding role, supporting the claim that beliefs themselves extend beyond the brain. Twin Otto and explanatory simplicity distinguish this thesis from merely historical externalism.

sections.title: Testing the memory–notebook analogy

source_span.end_text: Otto's notebook has all the relevant dispositions.

sections.summary: The authors consider differences in reliability, availability, bandwidth, perception, and consciousness between biological and external memory. They argue that these differences do not defeat the analogy once ordinary dispositional beliefs are admitted.

sections.title: Limits, social extension, and personal identity
sections.summary: Constancy, easy access, automatic endorsement, and possibly prior endorsement constrain which external resources constitute beliefs. The argument extends to trusted people, language, the self, and the ethical consequences of interference with cognitive environments.
